en: Having prostrated before Śiva, the supreme Lord of Death, I shall hereafter proclaim the initiation of knowledge; listen with concentrated minds. || 1 ||
Then, for the sake of liberation from the bondage of karma known as the impurity of the self and māyā, and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva-hood, knowledge proceeds from Śiva. (2)
Although that [reality] is one, it assumes multiplicity arising from the lotus-face of Śiva;
through the distinction between the supreme and the non-supreme, it proceeds by taking recourse to various objects.
Thus the Lord of the Gods, having summarized this supreme essence of the scripture in two aphorisms, spoke it again in detail.
Now, the soul, being initially bound and then liberated through initiation, is to be known as existing in three states:
the Kevala (isolated), the Sakala (with parts), and the Amala (stainless). || 5 ||

The bound soul (paśu) is insentient, all-pervading, eternal, devoid of qualities, inactive, powerless, subject to obstruction, incapable [of independent action], to be purified, to be awakened, and partless. || 6 ||
O twice-born ones, previously I have indeed described how this Self exists as being of the nature of illusion through these verse-compositions spoken from the mouth of my Guru. (7)
The experiencer, by virtue of being an enjoyer through various spreading enjoyments, is now declared to be the bound self (ātman) bound by the fetter of the kalās and other principles. 8.
The *kalā*, acting in accordance with the will of Śiva, enters into conjunction with that which was previously described as absolutely impure and immutable. (9)
Then, consciousness is empowered by *kalā*, its objects are revealed by *vidyā*, and it is colored by *rāga* through the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*). || 10 ||
On the path consisting of the principles (tattvas) from Māyā down to the earth, the person who is solely intent on enjoyment, remaining therein, experiences enjoyments. || 11 ||
Experience for this person consists of sensation characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth;
endowed with consciousness, the person undergoes that [sensation] due to karma. (12)
And through karma, bodies, objects,
and instruments come into being or cease to be for the sake of the experience of the enjoyer, so that his enjoyment may be fully accomplished.
Thus, like one situated in an illusory collyrium, the individual soul (aṇu), obscured by its own defects and enamored by them, attains identification with those illusory enjoyments. 14.

The wise declare that the bound self (baddhātman) is called "transmigrating," "possessing objects," "the enjoyer," "the knower of the field" (kṣetrajña), and also "embodied," and it is known as "sakala" (with parts). || 15 ||
In the past, by the will of Śiva, the infinite power of Śiva, which bestows the goals of Śiva,
that primordial power descends upon a person in his final birth.
From that union, his impurity—the cause of saṃsāra—is discharged.
When that is exhausted, there arises the desire to go toward the supreme, ultimate liberation.
Having approached the guide and had his bonds severed by initiation, he becomes stainless and free from further support, proceeding to union with Śiva. 18.
By this sequential yoga, having attained supreme isolation, one reaches a state beyond further existence due to being devoid of beginningless impurity. || 19 ||
Thus has the Self been fully described as abiding in all states;
now, O Brahman, the infinite net of bonds is being proclaimed.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Investigation of the Bound Soul (Paśu), in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṅgraha.
